course.title: AP World History: Modern

framework.name: InSPECT

framework.sourceNote: Based on the class Early Religions + InSPECT slides, pages 5-17.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Dar al-Islam around 1200–1450?
choices: Political authority divided among regional states, and each developed isolated religious law and scholarly networks.
Muslim political authority divided among states while religious and cultural links persisted.
The Abbasid caliph continued appointing most regional rulers, although sultans commanded local armies and taxes.
New Turkic states restored political unity by replacing Arabic and Persian traditions with one shared government.
questions.explanation: New states held political power, yet religious practices, legal traditions, commerce, and learning connected communities across their borders. Political fragmentation did not mean cultural isolation or continued direct Abbasid control.

questions.stimulus: A military ruler commands an army and controls taxation while recognizing the religious prestige of a caliph in Baghdad.
questions.prompt: Which development does this situation best illustrate?
choices: The caliph retained control of taxation while granting the sultan only ceremonial religious authority
Merchant elites replaced military rulers and caliphs as the main source of political legitimacy
Regional military rulers gained authority by abolishing the caliphate and rejecting all Abbasid institutions
A distinction between a sultan’s political power and a caliph’s religious prestige
questions.explanation: Seljuk rulers illustrate how sultans could hold practical military and political authority while Abbasid caliphs retained religious prestige. The tempting reverse arrangement assigns each figure the wrong kind of authority.

questions.prompt: How could the pilgrimage to Mecca help connect Muslim societies?
choices: It brought believers from different regions into contact through a shared religious practice.
It chiefly allowed rulers to negotiate alliances among independent Muslim states.
It imposed one legal interpretation on every Muslim region.
It strengthened regional sultans by letting each supervise a separate pilgrimage.
questions.explanation: Pilgrimage joined a shared religious obligation with travel and encounters across regions. Its unifying effect came from participation in the same practice, not political negotiations, one universal legal interpretation, or separate regional pilgrimages.

questions.stimulus: Records from a Muslim-ruled city show Jewish and Christian communities maintaining worship and participating in trade, while facing special taxes and legal restrictions.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion accounts for all the evidence?
choices: Religious minorities gained legal equality because their commercial activity made special taxes unnecessary.
Economic cooperation occurred only after Jewish and Christian residents abandoned public worship.
Religious coexistence could operate alongside unequal legal status.
Non-Muslims maintained worship but were excluded from the city’s commercial life by legal restrictions.
questions.explanation: The evidence includes continuing worship and trade as well as taxes and legal restrictions. A complete conclusion must recognize both coexistence and inequality instead of using one part of the evidence to erase the other.

questions.stimulus: A port community gradually adopts Islamic practices through contact with visiting merchants and a local Sufi teacher. No new army has taken control of the port.
questions.prompt: Which process best explains this change?
choices: Commercial contact that prepared the port for conversion after its conquest by an Abbasid army
Religious diffusion through commerce and teaching
State-sponsored conversion led by a local ruler seeking closer relations with Muslim merchants
Migration by Muslim merchants that replaced the port’s existing population and religious traditions
questions.explanation: The scenario gives evidence of trade and Sufi teaching but explicitly excludes military conquest. Contact could support gradual religious diffusion without state sponsorship or the replacement of the local population.

questions.prompt: Why should a historian distinguish the expansion of Muslim rule from the spread of Islam?
choices: The expansion of Muslim rule describes religious conversion, whereas the spread of Islam describes changing state borders.
Military conquest created Islamic states, while merchants affected commerce without influencing religious belief.
Islam could spread through trade beyond state borders, but Muslim rulers governed only communities that had already converted.
A Muslim government could rule non-Muslims, and Islam could spread beyond its political borders.
questions.explanation: Political control and religious change are different processes. Muslim states could rule non-Muslim subjects, while merchants and teachers could carry Islam beyond those states; neither process required the other to be complete.

questions.prompt: Which example most clearly illustrates intellectual innovation in the Islamic world?
choices: Al-Tusi developing mathematical and astronomical work at an observatory
Physicians in Cairo copying established medical manuals for storage in a hospital library
Scholars in Baghdad translating Greek philosophical works into Arabic without adding new commentary
Merchants carrying Indian mathematical texts to new scholarly markets across Dar al-Islam
questions.explanation: Al-Tusi’s mathematical and astronomical work added to knowledge. Copying, translating, and transporting texts are important forms of preservation or transfer, but innovation specifically develops new methods, explanations, or findings.

questions.stimulus: A student claims that the Mongol capture of Baghdad in 1258 ended intellectual activity everywhere in the Islamic world.
questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly challenges the claim?
choices: Abbasid caliphs had supported translation and scholarship in Baghdad before the Mongol conquest.
Ibn Rushd produced philosophical commentaries in al-Andalus during the twelfth century.
Al-Tusi conducted astronomical work under Mongol patronage, and Ibn Khaldun wrote in a later century.
Baghdad’s libraries contained works produced in earlier centuries.
questions.explanation: The claim concerns all intellectual activity after 1258, so evidence of later scholarship directly contradicts it. The other choices establish earlier achievements but do not prove that new intellectual work continued afterward.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best explains one route of intellectual exchange through Iberia?
choices: Greek texts → translation from Latin into Arabic in Iberia → replacement of Arabic scholarship by European universities
Arabic texts and commentaries → direct adoption by European scholars without translation → identical interpretations
European texts → translation into Arabic → use limited to Muslim rulers and excluded from Iberian scholarly communities
Arabic texts and commentaries → translation into Latin → wider use by European scholars
questions.explanation: Translation from Arabic into Latin allowed additional European readers to study earlier works and Arabic commentaries. Exchange widened access and debate rather than eliminating translation, producing identical interpretations, or restricting texts to rulers.

questions.prompt: What useful comparison links Islamic intellectual exchange with Chinese cultural influence in Korea and Japan?
choices: Both involved receiving societies adopting and adapting ideas across political boundaries.
Both crossed borders, but receiving societies copied foreign ideas without local adaptation.
Both required conquest and political control before cultural exchange could occur.
Both remained limited to rulers and scholars and did not reshape local traditions.
questions.explanation: In both cases, cultural influence crossed political borders and involved local choices. The key distinction is that receiving societies adapted ideas; exchange did not require conquest, exact copying, or direct imperial rule.

questions.prompt: Which state emerged when a military elite took power in Egypt in 1250?
choices: Song dynasty
Mamluk Sultanate
Delhi Sultanate
Abbasid Caliphate
questions.explanation: Mamluk leaders established their sultanate in Egypt in 1250. Delhi was a separate center of Muslim rule in northern India; the Song governed in China.

questions.prompt: What role did Sufi teachers play in the spread of Islam?
choices: They required all communities to abandon local languages.
They ended religious teaching outside Baghdad.
They introduced religious ideas through spiritual instruction and community relationships.
They united every Muslim state under a single sultan.
questions.explanation: Sufi teachers helped communicate Islam through spiritual practice and personal relationships. Their methods varied, and their influence did not depend on one unified state.

questions.prompt: Why did translating scholarly works into new languages matter?
choices: It removed the need for anyone to study earlier ideas.
It proved all societies held identical beliefs.
It ensured every translated idea remained unchanged forever.
It allowed new groups of readers to study, debate, and develop the ideas.
questions.explanation: Translation widened access to knowledge. Readers could interpret or build on ideas, so intellectual transfer could also support further innovation.

questions.prompt: The capture of Baudas described in the passage is best understood in the context of
choices: the rise of the Ottoman Empire in Anatolia and the Balkans
the expansion of the Mongol Empire into western Europe
the Crusades, in which European armies sought to control Jerusalem
the expansion of the Mongol Empire across Eurasia
questions.explanation: Hulagu, brother of Kublai Khan, led the Mongol campaign that took Baghdad in 1258.
choiceExplanations: The Ottomans rose later and did not take Baghdad until the 1500s.
The capture of Baghdad was part of Mongol expansion into Southwest Asia, not western Europe.
Crusader armies fought for the Levant, but Alaue (Hulagu) was a Mongol prince, not a crusader.
Hulagu, brother of Kublai Khan, led the Mongol campaign that took Baghdad in 1258.
questions.distinguisher: The Mongols did expand west, but their main campaigns into Europe did not take or hold western Europe; Hulagu's army moved into Southwest Asia.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant who traveled in Mongol-ruled Asia c. 1271–1295, account dictated to the writer Rustichello of Pisa, c. 1298, describing Baghdad
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1903), vol. 1, Book I, ch. 6. Project Gutenberg eBook #10636.
stimulusBlocks.note: Baudas is Baghdad. Saracens means Muslims. Alaue is Hulagu, brother of Kublai Khan, and the Calif was the Abbasid caliph. Baghdad fell to Hulagu in 1258; Polo gives the year as 1255.
stimulusBlocks.text:
Baudas is a great city, which used to be the seat of the Calif of all the Saracens in the world, just as Rome is the seat of the Pope of all the Christians. A very great river flows through the city, and by this you can descend to the Sea of India. There is a great traffic of merchants with their goods this way . . . .

In Baudas they weave many different kinds of silk stuffs and gold brocades . . . . It is the noblest and greatest city in all those regions.

Now it came to pass on a day in the year of Christ 1255, that the Lord of the Tartars of the Levant, whose name was Alaue, brother to the Great Kaan now reigning, gathered a mighty host and came up against Baudas and took it by storm. . . . Howbeit, since that time, there has been never another Calif, either at Baudas or anywhere else.

questions.prompt: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly challenge Polo's final claim in the passage?
choices: Mamluk sultans in Cairo defeated a Mongol army at Ayn Jalut in 1260 and halted its advance
Mamluk sultans in Cairo installed members of the Abbasid family as caliphs after 1261
Muslim scholars continued to work at observatories under Mongol rule
Baghdad remained a center of silk weaving after the Mongol conquest
questions.explanation: Polo claims there was never another caliph; the Mamluks' Abbasid caliphs in Cairo show that the office continued, though with little power.
choiceExplanations: Ayn Jalut checked Mongol expansion but says nothing about whether a caliph existed.
Polo claims there was never another caliph; the Mamluks' Abbasid caliphs in Cairo show that the office continued, though with little power.
Continued scholarship is true but does not address whether there were caliphs.
Silk weaving concerns Baghdad's economy, not the existence of the caliphate.
questions.distinguisher: Ayn Jalut is a real Mamluk victory, but Polo's claim is about caliphs, not about Mongol defeats.

questions.prompt: The passage best illustrates which of the following developments in Dar al-Islam?
choices: The weakening of Abbasid power by Seljuk Turks after 1200
The unification of Muslim lands under a single strong caliph
The final end of Abbasid political power in Baghdad
The conversion of the Mongol rulers of Persia to Christianity
questions.explanation: Hulagu's capture of Baghdad and the caliph's death ended Abbasid rule there.
choiceExplanations: Seljuk dominance began in the eleventh century, and the passage describes a Mongol conquest.
The passage describes the caliph's defeat and death, not unification.
Hulagu's capture of Baghdad and the caliph's death ended Abbasid rule there.
The Ilkhans of Persia eventually converted to Islam, not Christianity.
questions.distinguisher: Seljuk sultans did reduce the caliph's power, but before 1200; the passage shows the Mongol blow of 1258.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following best describes how new Islamic states emerged in this period?
choices: Military elites, many of Turkic origin, took power as caliphal authority weakened
European crusaders created Muslim client states in Egypt and India
Military elites, many of Turkic origin, ruled as caliphs in place of the Abbasids
Arab tribal leaders rebuilt the caliphate's authority in Baghdad
questions.explanation: Seljuks, Mamluks, and the Delhi sultans were military elites who rose as the caliph lost power.
choiceExplanations: Seljuks, Mamluks, and the Delhi sultans were military elites who rose as the caliph lost power.
Crusaders did not create the Mamluk or Delhi states.
These rulers used the title sultan; the passage says the caliph remained a religious figurehead.
The passage describes Turkic and Mamluk military rulers, not a revival led by Arab tribes.
questions.distinguisher: The Seljuks ruled as sultans and kept the caliph as a figurehead; they did not take the title of caliph.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.2, KC-3.2.I: as the Abbasid Caliphate fragmented, new Islamic political entities emerged, most of which were dominated by Turkic peoples
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the rise of military states in Dar al-Islam, c. 1000–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
By the eleventh century the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad had lost most of his practical power. Seljuk Turks took control of much of Southwest Asia and ruled as sultans while leaving the caliph as a religious figurehead. In Egypt, the Mamluks, soldiers originally purchased as enslaved boys and trained for war, seized power in 1250 and defeated a Mongol army at Ayn Jalut in 1260. In northern India, Turkic commanders founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.

These states were governed by military elites who were often culturally different from the populations they ruled. They gained legitimacy by defending Muslim lands, supporting religious scholars, and building mosques and schools.

questions.prompt: The rulers described in the passage were most similar to which of the following in how they gained legitimacy?
choices: Ethiopian kings, who supported religious institutions such as monasteries
Inca rulers, who recorded labor obligations on knotted cords
Song emperors, who claimed authority through the Mandate of Heaven and Confucian learning
Mexica rulers, who used tribute lists to record conquered towns
questions.explanation: Like sultans who built mosques and supported scholars, Ethiopian kings sponsored monasteries to tie their rule to faith.
choiceExplanations: Like sultans who built mosques and supported scholars, Ethiopian kings sponsored monasteries to tie their rule to faith.
Khipu recorded obligations; they were a record-keeping tool, not a claim to legitimacy.
Song legitimacy used Confucian ideas, which is related, but the passage stresses patronage of religious institutions.
Tribute lists were an administrative tool, not a source of religious legitimacy.
questions.distinguisher: Song rulers also used ideas to justify rule, but Confucianism is a philosophy of government, not support for a religious institution like mosques or monasteries.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the author's view of scholars in Dar al-Islam?
choices: They preserved older works but rejected ideas from India
They mainly copied Greek texts without adding new ideas
They preserved older works and also produced new knowledge
They stopped working after the Mongol conquests of the 1250s
questions.explanation: Translation preserved older knowledge, and figures such as al-Tusi added new models and findings.
choiceExplanations: The passage lists Indian works among those translated into Arabic.
The passage says scholars “did more than preserve,” giving al-Tusi and medical writers as examples.
Translation preserved older knowledge, and figures such as al-Tusi added new models and findings.
Al-Tusi worked at Maragha under Mongol rulers, so scholarship continued.
questions.distinguisher: Preservation is part of the story, but the passage names Indian works among those translated.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.2, KC-3.2.II.A.i: Muslim states and empires encouraged significant intellectual innovations and transfers
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how historians describe scholarship in Dar al-Islam, c. 800–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
Abbasid patronage in Baghdad, associated with the House of Wisdom, supported the translation of Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic. Later scholars did more than preserve these texts. Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, working at the Maragha observatory under Mongol rulers, refined models of planetary motion, and physicians wrote medical encyclopedias based on hospital practice.

In Iberia, Muslim, Jewish, and Christian scholars worked with Arabic texts. After Christian kingdoms captured cities such as Toledo, translators there turned Arabic works on philosophy, medicine, and mathematics into Latin, and these translations reached European universities.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a direct effect of the developments in Iberia described in the second paragraph?
choices: European universities gained access to Chinese printing techniques
European universities gained access to Greek and Arabic learning
Arabic replaced Latin as the language of European universities
Muslim rulers expanded their control over all of Iberia
questions.explanation: Latin translations from Toledo brought Aristotle and Arabic science into European universities.
choiceExplanations: The translations described concerned philosophy, medicine, and mathematics, not printing.
Latin translations from Toledo brought Aristotle and Arabic science into European universities.
Latin remained the language of European universities; translation moved texts into Latin.
The passage describes Christian kingdoms capturing cities such as Toledo, the opposite of Muslim expansion.
questions.distinguisher: Translation moved books between languages, but the passage concerns philosophy, medicine, and mathematics, not printing.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would most directly support the author's argument in the first paragraph?
choices: Evidence that Islamic astronomers copied Greek star tables exactly
Evidence that the House of Wisdom was destroyed in 1258
Evidence that Arabic texts were later printed in Europe
Evidence that Islamic astronomers corrected earlier Greek models
questions.explanation: Corrections to Greek models show scholars going beyond what they inherited, the author's central claim.
choiceExplanations: Copying would support preservation, not the claim that scholars did more than preserve.
Destruction in 1258 says nothing about whether scholars added new knowledge.
Later printing concerns the spread of texts, not original contributions.
Corrections to Greek models show scholars going beyond what they inherited, the author's central claim.
questions.distinguisher: Exact copying would show preservation only; the argument is that scholars added something new.
